claim: A missense mutation of collagen type VIII alpha 2 chain (COL8A2) gene leads to early-onset Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD).
source: A missense mutation of collagen type VIII alpha 2 chain (COL8A2) gene leads to early-onset Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD), which progressively impairs vision through the loss of corneal endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the literature, referenced in the introduction with citations (Gottsch et al., 2005; Biswas et al., 2001; Vedana et al., 2016).

claim: Early-onset FECD progressively impairs vision through the loss of corneal endothelial cells.
source: A missense mutation of collagen type VIII alpha 2 chain (COL8A2) gene leads to early-onset Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD), which progressively impairs vision through the loss of corneal endothelial cells.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of FECD supported by established medical knowledge.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based postnatal gene editing achieves structural and functional rescue in a mouse model of FECD.
source: We demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-based postnatal gene editing achieves structural and functional rescue in a mouse model of FECD.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 7-10.

claim: A single intraocular injection of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA efficiently knocked down mutant COL8A2 expression in corneal endothelial cells.
source: A single intraocular injection of an adenovirus encoding both the Cas9 gene and guide RNA (Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA) efficiently knocked down mutant COL8A2 expression in corneal endothelial cells, prevented endothelial cell loss, and rescued corneal endothelium pumping function in adult Col8a2 mutant mice.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing reduced COL8A2 protein expression.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA prevented endothelial cell loss in adult Col8a2 mutant mice.
source: A single intraocular injection of an adenovirus encoding both the Cas9 gene and guide RNA (Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA) efficiently knocked down mutant COL8A2 expression in corneal endothelial cells, prevented endothelial cell loss, and rescued corneal endothelium pumping function in adult Col8a2 mutant mice.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7 showing preserved corneal endothelial cell density.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA rescued corneal endothelium pumping function in adult Col8a2 mutant mice.
source: A single intraocular injection of an adenovirus encoding both the Cas9 gene and guide RNA (Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA) efficiently knocked down mutant COL8A2 expression in corneal endothelial cells, prevented endothelial cell loss, and rescued corneal endothelium pumping function in adult Col8a2 mutant mice.
evidence: Supported by functional data in Figure 10 showing improved de-swelling rates.

claim: There were no adverse sequelae on histology or electroretinography following Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA treatment.
source: There were no adverse sequelae on histology or electroretinography.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4 showing normal histology and ERG.

claim: Col8a2 start codon disruption represents a non-surgical strategy to prevent vision loss in early-onset FECD.
source: Col8a2 start codon disruption represents a non-surgical strategy to prevent vision loss in early-onset FECD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing structural and functional rescue.

claim: Ad-Cas9-gRNA can restore the phenotype in adult post-mitotic cells.
source: As this demonstrates the ability of Ad-Cas9-gRNA to restore the phenotype in adult post-mitotic cells, this method may be widely applicable to adult-onset diseases, even in tissues affected with disorders of non-reproducing cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by the successful treatment of corneal endothelial cells, which are post-mitotic.

claim: This method may be widely applicable to adult-onset diseases in tissues with non-reproducing cells.
source: As this demonstrates the ability of Ad-Cas9-gRNA to restore the phenotype in adult post-mitotic cells, this method may be widely applicable to adult-onset diseases, even in tissues affected with disorders of non-reproducing cells.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the current findings.

claim: FECD is the leading cause of corneal transplantation in industrialized societies.
source: Fuchs' endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD), which is characterized by progressive loss of corneal endothelial cells, is the leading cause of corneal transplantation in industrialized societies (EBAA, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to EBAA, 2016.

claim: The only available treatment for advanced FECD is corneal transplantation.
source: Currently, the only available treatment for advanced FECD is corneal transplantation, which entails significant risks (e.g., infection, hemorrhage, rejection, glaucoma) both during surgery and during the lifetime of the patient (Mitry et al., 2014; Sugar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitry et al., 2014 and Sugar et al., 2015.

claim: Corneal transplantation entails significant risks including infection, hemorrhage, rejection, and glaucoma.
source: Currently, the only available treatment for advanced FECD is corneal transplantation, which entails significant risks (e.g., infection, hemorrhage, rejection, glaucoma) both during surgery and during the lifetime of the patient (Mitry et al., 2014; Sugar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitry et al., 2014 and Sugar et al., 2015.

claim: A missense mutation of the COL8A2 gene in humans causes early-onset Fuchs' dystrophy.
source: A missense mutation of the collagen 8A2 (COL8A2) gene in humans causes early-onset Fuchs' dystrophy (Gottsch et al., 2005; Biswas et al., 2001; Vedana et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gottsch et al., 2005; Biswas et al., 2001; Vedana et al., 2016.

claim: Other mutations within the ZEB1/TCF8 locus and TCF4 trinucleotide repeats are associated with Fuchs' dystrophy.
source: Although other mutations within the ZEB1/TCF8 locus and TCF4 trinucleotide repeats are associated with Fuchs' dystrophy (Riazuddin et al., 2010; Igo et al., 2012; Aldave et al., 2013; Stamler et al., 2013; Nanda et al., 2014; Mootha et al., 2015; Nakano et al., 2015; Afshari et al., 2017; Kuot et al., 2017), only the Col8a2 missense mutant mouse has successfully recapitulated its key features.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Riazuddin et al., 2010; Igo et al., 2012; Aldave et al., 2013; Stamler et al., 2013; Nanda et al., 2014; Mootha et al., 2015; Nakano et al., 2015; Afshari et al., 2017; Kuot et al., 2017).

claim: Only the Col8a2 missense mutant mouse has successfully recapitulated key features of FECD.
source: Although other mutations within the ZEB1/TCF8 locus and TCF4 trinucleotide repeats are associated with Fuchs' dystrophy (Riazuddin et al., 2010; Igo et al., 2012; Aldave et al., 2013; Stamler et al., 2013; Nanda et al., 2014; Mootha et al., 2015; Nakano et al., 2015; Afshari et al., 2017; Kuot et al., 2017), only the Col8a2 missense mutant mouse has successfully recapitulated its key features.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of mouse models in the field.

claim: Knockout mice lacking Col8a2 alone or combined with homozygous Col8a1 knockout mutation do not develop FECD.
source: Knockout mice lacking Col8a2 alone or combined with a homozygous Col8a1 knockout mutation do not develop FECD (Hopfer et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hopfer et al., 2005.

claim: Double Col8a2/Col8a1 knockout mice exhibited corneal biomechanical weakening without endothelial loss.
source: Although the double knockouts exhibited corneal biomechanical weakening (without endothelial loss), Col8a2 knockouts showed no apparent phenotype.
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited (Hopfer et al., 2005).

claim: Col8a2 knockout mice showed no apparent phenotype.
source: Although the double knockouts exhibited corneal biomechanical weakening (without endothelial loss), Col8a2 knockouts showed no apparent phenotype.
evidence: This is based on previous studies cited (Hopfer et al., 2005).

claim: Col8a2 mutant knock-in mice carrying Q455K and L450W mutations displayed corneal endothelial excrescences (guttae) and endothelial cell loss.
source: In contrast, Col8a2 mutant knock-in mice carrying the Q455K and L450W mutations associated with early-onset FECD in human patients displayed corneal endothelial excrescences known as guttae, as well as the endothelial cell loss, which are hallmarks of human FECD (Meng et al., 2013; Jun et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meng et al., 2013 and Jun et al., 2012.

claim: Guttae and endothelial cell loss are hallmarks of human FECD.
source: In contrast, Col8a2 mutant knock-in mice carrying the Q455K and L450W mutations associated with early-onset FECD in human patients displayed corneal endothelial excrescences known as guttae, as well as the endothelial cell loss, which are hallmarks of human FECD (Meng et al., 2013; Jun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about FECD pathology.

claim: COL8A2 protein is not essential to corneal function.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that COL8A2 protein is not essential to corneal function, yet is causally responsible for FECD via mutant dominant gain-of-function activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that Col8a2 knockout mice show no apparent phenotype.

claim: COL8A2 is causally responsible for FECD via mutant dominant gain-of-function activity.
source: Taken together, these studies suggest that COL8A2 protein is not essential to corneal function, yet is causally responsible for FECD via mutant dominant gain-of-function activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrast between knockout and knock-in mouse phenotypes.

claim: px330-MsCol8a2gRNA1 creates an indel in mouse NIH3T3 cells.
source: As expected, px330-MsCol8a2gRNA1 creates an indel in mouse NIH3T3 cells (Figure 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel electrophoresis in Figure 1b showing an undigested band.

claim: Co-transfection of px330-MsCol8a2gRNA1 with px330-MsCol8a2gRNA2 or px330-MsCol8a2gRNA3 resulted in an extra PCR band.
source: Co-transfection of px330-MsCol8a2gRNA1 with px330-MsCol8a2gRNA2 or px330-MsCol8a2gRNA3 resulted in an extra PCR band (Figure 1c).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1c gel electrophoresis.

claim: The indels by px330-MsCol8A2gRNA1 were confirmed by sequencing.
source: The indels by px330-MsCol8A2gRNA1 were confirmed by sequencing (Figure 1d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1d Sanger sequencing results.

claim: Adenovirus-GFP showed efficient green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression in corneal endothelium.
source: In fact, we found adenovirus-GFP showed efficient green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression in corneal endothelium (Figure 2a).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence microscopy in Figure 2a.

claim: Anterior chamber injection of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA induces indels in the corneal endothelium but not in the epithelium or stroma.
source: This strongly suggests that the anterior chamber injection of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA induces indels in the corneal endothelium but not in the epithelium or stroma.
evidence: Supported by PCR and restriction enzyme digestion data in Figure 2b showing indels only in endothelium/stroma samples.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected corneas exhibited reduced COL8A2 protein expression in corneal endothelium but not corneal epithelium.
source: As predicted, Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected corneas exhibited reduced COL8A2 protein expression in corneal endothelium but not corneal epithelium.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining in Figure 3 and quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The intensity of COL8A2 staining in corneal endothelium layer significantly decreased at 0.63 × 10^7 vg and 0.25 × 10^8 vg of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA compared to the no-injection control.
source: While the epithelium layer did not show any significant difference, the intensity of COL8A2 staining in corneal endothelium layer significantly decreased at 0.63 × 107 vg and 0.25 × 108 vg of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA compared to the no-injection control.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: Corneal transparency, corneal thickness, and histopathology appeared normal at low titers of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA.
source: Corneal transparency, corneal thickness, and histopathology appeared normal at low titers (Figure 4a–d), and ZO-1 immunolabeling detected reduced endothelial density in corneal flat mounts after injecting 1.0 × 108 vg (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4a-d with OCT and histology images.

claim: ZO-1 immunolabeling detected reduced endothelial density in corneal flat mounts after injecting 1.0 × 10^8 vg of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA.
source: Corneal transparency, corneal thickness, and histopathology appeared normal at low titers (Figure 4a–d), and ZO-1 immunolabeling detected reduced endothelial density in corneal flat mounts after injecting 1.0 × 108 vg (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4e-f with immunofluorescence and quantification.

claim: A higher titer (4.0 × 10^8 vg) of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA devastated the mouse corneal endothelium, inducing corneal opacity and edema in C57BL/6J mice.
source: A higher titer (4.0 × 108 vg) devastated the mouse corneal endothelium, inducing corneal opacity and edema in C57BL/6J mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 0.25 × 10^8 vg, neither TNFα nor IFNγ was upregulated 4 weeks after Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA injection.
source: At 0.25 × 108 vg, neither tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) nor interferon gamma (IFNγ) was upregulated 4 weeks after Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by immunostaining in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA did not suppress retinal function as monitored by electroretinography.
source: Moreover, we confirmed that Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA did not suppress retinal function, as monitored by electroretinography (ERG), or damage the retinal structure, as visualized by hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 with ERG measurements.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA did not damage the retinal structure as visualized by hematoxylin-eosin staining.
source: Moreover, we confirmed that Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA did not suppress retinal function, as monitored by electroretinography (ERG), or damage the retinal structure, as visualized by hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4a with histology.

claim: Anterior chamber injection of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA did not induce liver or kidney damage or inflammation.
source: Finally, anterior chamber injection of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA did not induce liver or kidney damage or inflammation, as visualized by HE staining of hepatic and renal tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4b with histology.

claim: The indel rate was 23.7 ± 4.5% in mouse corneal endothelium.
source: We found that the indel rate was 23.7 ± 4.5% in mouse corneal endothelium (Table 1).
evidence: Determined by deep sequencing and shown in Table 1.

claim: Most insertions were 1 bp insertions (19.8 ± 4.0% in total reads).
source: Most insertions were 1 bp insertions (19.8 ± 4.0% in total reads, Figure 5a), while 2 bp deletions were the most frequent (1.0 ± 0.3% in total reads, Figure 5b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5a with frequency distribution.

claim: 2 bp deletions were the most frequent deletions (1.0 ± 0.3% in total reads).
source: Most insertions were 1 bp insertions (19.8 ± 4.0% in total reads, Figure 5a), while 2 bp deletions were the most frequent (1.0 ± 0.3% in total reads, Figure 5b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5b with frequency distribution.

claim: A or T insertion was predominant, with the proportion of A:T:G:C being 48.7:44.6:1.8:4.9.
source: We, moreover, found that A or T insertion was predominant, with the proportion of A:T:G:C being 48.7:44.6:1.8:4.9 (Table 2).
evidence: Shown in Table 2 with nucleotide insertion frequencies.

claim: Adenine insertion (9.4 ± 1.9% in total reads) produced a cryptic ATG start codon.
source: Adenine insertion (9.4 ± 1.9% in total reads) produced a cryptic ATG start codon (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with sequence diagram.

claim: Adenine insertion changes G to C at the −3 position of the start codon.
source: This insertion changes G to C at the −3 position (A in ATG as +1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: G or A at the −3 position is important for translational commencement (Kozak sequence).
source: Since previous studies have indicated that G or A at the −3 position is important for translational commencement, which is known as a Kozak sequence (Kozak, 1984; Rual et al., 2004), a consequent reduction in protein expression by the disruption of Kozak/ATG sequence would be predicted.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kozak, 1984 and Rual et al., 2004.

claim: Disruption of Kozak/ATG sequence would result in reduction in protein expression.
source: Since previous studies have indicated that G or A at the −3 position is important for translational commencement, which is known as a Kozak sequence (Kozak, 1984; Rual et al., 2004), a consequent reduction in protein expression by the disruption of Kozak/ATG sequence would be predicted.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about Kozak sequences.

claim: The normalized indel rate (proportion of endothelial cells with indels) is 102.5 ± 16.3%.
source: From this calculation, the normalized indel rate (proportion of endothelial cells with indels) is 102.5 ± 16.3%.
evidence: Calculated from data in Table 3 accounting for stromal cell contamination.

claim: Cas9 and gRNA expressions were high at 0.63 × 10^7 and 2.5 × 10^7 vg of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA.
source: We found that Cas9 and gRNA expressions were high at 0.63 × 107 and 2.5 × 107 vg (Figure 6a–b) and that these doses of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA demonstrated a significant decrease of COL8A2 in corneal endothelium as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6a-b with RT-PCR data.

claim: In C57BL/6J mice, the normal Col8a2 mRNA (no indel) rates were 58.7 ± 11.4% (6.3 × 10^6 vg) and 56.1 ± 42.9% (25 × 10^6 vg).
source: In C57BL/6J mice, the normal Col8a2 mRNA (no indel) rates were 58.7 ± 11.4% (6.3 × 106 vg) and 56.1 ± 42.9% (25 × 106 vg), while in Col8a2Q455K mice, the normal Col8a2 mRNA (no indel) rates were 67.5 ± 19.0% (6.3 × 106 vg) and 35.4 ± 33.3% (25 × 106 vg) (Figure 6c).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6c with RT-PCR data.

claim: In Col8a2Q455K mice, the normal Col8a2 mRNA (no indel) rates were 67.5 ± 19.0% (6.3 × 10^6 vg) and 35.4 ± 33.3% (25 × 10^6 vg).
source: In C57BL/6J mice, the normal Col8a2 mRNA (no indel) rates were 58.7 ± 11.4% (6.3 × 106 vg) and 56.1 ± 42.9% (25 × 106 vg), while in Col8a2Q455K mice, the normal Col8a2 mRNA (no indel) rates were 67.5 ± 19.0% (6.3 × 106 vg) and 35.4 ± 33.3% (25 × 106 vg) (Figure 6c).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6c with RT-PCR data.

claim: Cas9 mRNA and gRNA were positively correlated.
source: Furthermore, Cas9 mRNA and gRNA were positively correlated (Figure 6d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6d with correlation plot.

claim: Cas9/gRNA and normal Col8a2 mRNA rate were inversely correlated.
source: On the other hand, Cas9/gRNA and normal Col8a2 mRNA rate were inversely correlated (Figure 6e and d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6e-f with correlation plots.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected eyes showed slower reduction of corneal endothelium than non-injected eyes in Col8a2Q455K/Q455K mice.
source: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected eyes showed slower reduction of corneal endothelium than the non-injected eyes (Figure 7b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7b with time course data of endothelial cell density.

claim: Intraocular injection of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA significantly rescued corneal endothelium in Col8a2Q455K/Q455K mice.
source: We found that intraocular injection of Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA significantly rescued corneal endothelium in Col8a2Q455K/Q455K mice (Figure 7d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7d with quantification of endothelial cell density.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected corneas demonstrated significantly higher corneal endothelium density than non-injected FECD eyes as confirmed by Alizarin red staining.
source: This was confirmed by Alizarin red staining (Figure 7e), which demonstrated a significantly higher corneal endothelium density in Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected corneas than in non-injected FECD eyes (Figure 7f).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7e-f with Alizarin red staining and quantification.

claim: All four individual Col8a2Q455K/Q455K mice showed significant improvements in corneal endothelial cell density by Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA treatment.
source: Analysis of paired corneas (injected and non-injected in the same mouse) showed significant improvements in corneal endothelial cell density by Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA treatment in all four individual mice (Figure 8a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8a with paired analysis.

claim: The morphology of the corneal endothelium, as monitored by hexagonality and coefficient of variation (COV) of its density, were improved considerably by Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA.
source: The morphology of the corneal endothelium, as monitored by hexagonality, and coefficient of variation (COV) of its density were improved considerably (Figure 8c–d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 8c-d with quantification of hexagonality and COV.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA decreased the formation of guttae-like structures compared to control as demonstrated by in vivo corneal OCT.
source: In vivo corneal optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated that Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA decreased the formation of guttae-like structures compared to control (Figure 9a–b), which was confirmed by histology (Figure 9c–d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 9a-b with OCT images and quantification.

claim: The reduction in guttae-like structures by Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA was confirmed by histology.
source: In vivo corneal optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrated that Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA decreased the formation of guttae-like structures compared to control (Figure 9a–b), which was confirmed by histology (Figure 9c–d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 9c-d with PAS staining.

claim: Col8a2Q455K/Q455K corneas did not develop edema or opacity even at 1 year of age despite reduced endothelial density.
source: Surprisingly, Col8a2Q455K/Q455K corneas did not develop edema or opacity even at 1 year of age despite reduced endothelial density (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1 with corneal thickness measurements.

claim: Direct application of a 0 mOsm/l solution induced epithelial rather than stromal swelling.
source: As direct application of a 0 mOsm/l solution was found to induce epithelial rather than stromal swelling (Figure 10—figure supplement 2), we performed epithelial debridement to eliminate any confounding epithelial effects (Figure 10a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2 with OCT measurements.

claim: 600–700 mOsm/l solution produced maximal corneal swelling effect, with quadrupling of the stromal thickness.
source: Application of an osmolar range of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) solutions (Figure 10b) produced a range of swelling volumes, with 600–700 mOsm/l solution producing the maximal effect, with quadrupling of the stromal thickness (Figure 10b–c).
evidence: Shown in Figure 10b-c with OCT images and thickness measurements.

claim: The epithelial layer functions as a barrier to maintain stromal thickness.
source: Thus, the epithelial layer functions as a barrier to maintain stromal thickness, whereas hypertonic solutions seem to induce aqueous humor ingression into the cornea.
evidence: This is inferred from the swelling experiments showing epithelial effects.

claim: Hypertonic solutions induce aqueous humor ingression into the cornea.
source: Thus, the epithelial layer functions as a barrier to maintain stromal thickness, whereas hypertonic solutions seem to induce aqueous humor ingression into the cornea.
evidence: This is inferred from the swelling experiments with hypertonic solutions.

claim: The rate of de-swelling in non-injected Col8a2Q455K/Q455K corneas was significantly delayed compared to C57BL/6J control corneas.
source: Successive corneal OCT images showed that the rate of de-swelling in non-injected Col8a2Q455K/Q455K corneas was significantly delayed compared to C57BL/6J control corneas.
evidence: Shown in Figure 10d-e with time course OCT measurements.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected Col8a2Q455K/Q455K corneas demonstrated de-swelling rates similar to C57BL/6J corneas.
source: In contrast, Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA-injected Col8a2Q455K/Q455K corneas demonstrated de-swelling rates similar to C57BL/6J corneas (Figure 10d–e).
evidence: Shown in Figure 10d-e with time course OCT measurements.

claim: Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA rescued corneal endothelial function in FECD mice.
source: Thus, Ad-Cas9-Col8a2gRNA rescued corneal endothelial function in FECD mice.
evidence: This is concluded from the de-swelling experiments showing functional rescue.

claim: Most insertions by CRISPR/Cas9 were single insertions of adenine, creating a cryptic start codon without frame shift.
source: We found that most of the insertions were single insertions of adenine, creating a cryptic start codon without frame shift (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: Disruption of the Kozak sequence effectively reduces protein expression without complications such as non-functional or frame-shifted protein production.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that disruption of the Kozak sequence effectively reduces protein expression without complications such as non-functional or frame-shifted protein production.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that adenine insertion disrupts the Kozak sequence and the observed reduction in COL8A2 protein.

claim: Kozak sequence disruption by CRISPR/Cas9 targeting may provide a viable option for gene knockdown.
source: Hence, Kozak sequence disruption by CRISPR/Cas9 targeting may provide a viable option for gene knockdown.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful knockdown achieved in this study.

claim: The majority of potential off-target sites with homology were in non-coding sequences.
source: We identified 13 potential off-target sites with homology, the majority of which were in non-coding sequences and other regions in genes of uncertain function.
evidence: Determined by digenome sequencing analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: One potential coding exonic off-target sequence was found in the ACAN gene.
source: We found one potential coding exonic off-target sequence in the ACAN gene.
evidence: Identified in digenome analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: ACAN expression was not observed in previously published RNAseq data of human corneal endothelium.
source: Although several cartilage-bone-related diseases are caused by mutations of ACAN coding region, its expression was not observed in previously published RNAseq data of human corneal endothelium (Wieben et al., 2018; Wieben et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wieben et al., 2018 and Wieben et al., 2019.

claim: The ACAN off-target indel is unlikely to affect corneal function.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that this off-target indel would affect corneal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ACAN expression in corneal endothelium.

claim: Off-target sequences were found in the intron of SV2C and KAT6B genes.
source: We found off-target sequences in the intron of two genes, SV2C (Synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2C) and KAT6B.
evidence: Identified in digenome analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: SV2C is rarely expressed in human corneal endothelium.
source: SV2C is involved in synaptic function throughout the brain (Dunn et al., 2017), but it is rarely expressed in human corneal endothelium (Wieben et al., 2018; Wieben et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wieben et al., 2018 and Wieben et al., 2019.

claim: The observed KAT6B off-target site is located over 11,000 bp from the exon–intron boundary.
source: The observed KAT6B off-target site is located over 11,000 bp from the exon–intron boundary.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the genomic location analysis.

claim: The off-target mutation in KAT6B is unlikely to cause corneal dysfunction.
source: Hence, the off-target mutation in KAT6B is unlikely to cause corneal dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the distance of the off-target site from splice junctions.

claim: Two additional off-target candidates were found in the intron of non-coding RNAs, SRGAP2-AS1 and LMO7-AS1.
source: Two additional off-target candidates were found in the intron of non-coding RNAs, SRGAP2-AS1 and LMO7-AS1.
evidence: Identified in digenome analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: The functions of SRGAP2-AS1 and LMO7-AS1 are unknown.
source: Non-coding RNAs are sometimes known to have various functions in gene regulation, but the functions of SRGAP2-AS1 and LMO7-AS1 are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: All other off-target candidates are located in intergenic regions.
source: All other off-target candidates are located in intergenic regions.
evidence: Identified in digenome analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: The risk of intergenic mutations inducing deleterious effects would be low compared with exonic or intronic mutations.
source: Compared with exonic or intronic mutations, the risk of intergenic mutations inducing deleterious effects would be low.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about mutation effects.

claim: Testing in large animals such as non-human primates should be performed prior to any clinical testing of in vivo CRISPR/cas9 treatment for humans.
source: However, testing in large animals such as non-human primates should be performed prior to any clinical testing of in vivo CRISPR/cas9 treatment for humans.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on standard preclinical development practices.

claim: Eight potential off-target sites without homology or PAM sequence were found.
source: Eight potential off-target sites without homology or PAM sequence were found, but we speculate these are likely random errors since the non-gRNA control also showed four potential off-target sites.
evidence: Identified in digenome analysis shown in Table 5.

claim: The eight potential off-target sites without homology are likely random errors.
source: Eight potential off-target sites without homology or PAM sequence were found, but we speculate these are likely random errors since the non-gRNA control also showed four potential off-target sites.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of similar sites in the control.

claim: Previous papers have achieved in vivo editing in post-mitotic neurons using dual AAV to co-infect cells with Cas9 machinery.

claim: The efficiency of homologous recombination by dual AAV delivery is 10–12%.
source: Although AAV has the advantages of low immunogenicity and toxicity, the low efficiency of HR by dual AAV delivery (10–12%) (Nishiyama et al., 2017) is unrealistic as a treatment approach, and the complexity of two vectors makes targeting efficacy assessment and clinical development challenging.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nishiyama et al., 2017.

source: There are several common viruses such as adeno-associated virus and lentivirus, but previous studies have indicated that only adenovirus demonstrates efficient gene transfer to corneal endothelium, in vivo.
evidence: This is based on previous studies and confirmed by the GFP expression data in Figure 2a.

claim: The strategy of targeting the start codon is sufficient for blocking gene expression at the translational level.
source: The strategy of targeting the start codon is sufficient for blocking gene expression at the translational level.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful knockdown of COL8A2 protein shown in Figure 3.

claim: Targeting the start codon minimizes the risk of missense mutations that result in viable mutant proteins with unknown activity.
source: The appeal of this strategy, as opposed to correcting the mutation through homologous recombination (HR), is that poor efficiency of CRISPR-based HR would result in a majority of sequence changes comprising insertions/deletions (indels). Consequently, the farther one targets downstream from the start codon, the greater the risk of missense mutations that result in viable mutant proteins with unknown activity. By targeting inside or near the start codon, this risk is minimized.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the advantages of the start codon targeting strategy.

claim: Poor efficiency of CRISPR-based homologous recombination results in a majority of sequence changes comprising insertions/deletions.
